identity.title: Recent biotechnological advances and technology readiness level of natural products derived from marine fungi.

content.abstract: Bioprospecting involves the systematic exploration of natural resources to identify bioactive secondary metabolites with potential for development into commercially valuable products. In this review, more than a hundred bioactive compounds derived from marine fungi were analysed, with emphasis on their chemical diversity, biological activities, commercialisation status, economic relevance, and Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs). The compounds represented diverse metabolite classes, including polyketides, alkaloids, terpenoids, peptides, azaphilones, and other bioactive secondary metabolites with pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, cosmeceutical, industrial, and environmental applications. Among the reviewed compounds, only approximately 10-20 have been marketed, while the majority remain at early stages of development. TRL assessment showed that most marine fungal-derived products are concentrated at TRL 1-3, a smaller number of compounds and bioprocesses have progressed to TRL 4-5, and highly commercialised products reach TRL 9. In India, pharmaceutical applications involving anticancer, antimicrobial, and antiviral compounds were assessed at TRL 3-5, nutraceuticals at TRL 5-7, cosmeceuticals at TRL 6-8, and industrial enzymes at TRL 7-9. The main barriers to commercialisation were low and unstable metabolite yields, structural complexity, regulatory and bioprospecting constraints, inadequate translational investment and industrial infrastructure, and high financial and technical risks during late-stage development. Integrated approaches including strain improvement, fermentation optimization, chemoenzymatic synthesis, OSMAC, in-situ product removal, genome mining, metabolic engineering, Chemi-genomic approaches, and CRISPR/Cas-based pathway engineering offer opportunities to improve production and increase TRLs. Overall, the findings demonstrate a substantial discovery-to-commercialization gap in marine fungal biotechnology. Advancing strain development, scalable bioprocessing, safety and regulatory validation, synthetic biology, industrial partnerships, and translational infrastructure is essential to convert promising low-TRL discoveries into commercially viable products and strengthen the contribution of marine fungi to a sustainable circular bioeconomy.
